Tenacity is the quality of firmly refusing to give up — even when things are extremely difficult, painful, or discouraging. It is the inner grip that keeps a person going when most others would have long since stopped. Think of it as a combination of persistence, toughness, and willpower, all fused into one sustained refusal to let go of a goal or effort.
What it looks like in real life

Imagine a scientist who runs the same experiment hundreds of times and keeps failing. Instead of quitting, she studies every failure, adjusts her method, and tries again — for years if necessary. Or picture an athlete who trains through injuries, defeats, and setbacks, never losing sight of what she is working toward. That unwillingness to surrender, that powerful forward push through repeated difficulty, is exactly what we call tenacity.

It is worth noting that tenacity implies a high degree of persistence — not just ordinary effort. You would not use this word to describe someone who tried twice and kept going. Tenacity is reserved for situations where the difficulty is real, the struggle is prolonged, and the person's refusal to quit is remarkable.
Why it is almost always a compliment

Tenacity carries a strongly positive meaning. When someone says "she showed extraordinary tenacity," they are expressing deep admiration. Society celebrates tenacity because virtually every significant achievement — in science, sport, art, business, and beyond — comes from people who refused to stop when things got hard. Calling someone tenacious is one of the finer things you can say about their character.
How it differs from similar words

This is where precision matters, because tenacity is often confused with related words.

Persistence means continuing to do something again and again. Tenacity includes persistence but adds emotional toughness and a sense of struggle — it suggests the person is holding on in the face of something genuinely hard, not just repeating a comfortable action.

Determination is the strong mental decision that you will not fail. Think of it as the starting point. Tenacity is what comes after that decision: the day-after-day, month-after-month sustaining of effort through every obstacle. Determination is the resolve; tenacity is the endurance.

Stubbornness is where many learners get confused, because it sounds similar. The key difference: stubbornness means refusing to change even when you are wrong — it is clinging to something when you should let go. Tenacity means refusing to quit even when things are hard — it is clinging to something worthy when quitting would be easier. Stubbornness is generally seen as a flaw; tenacity is almost always admired.

Resilience means the ability to recover and bounce back after a setback. Tenacity and resilience often appear together, but resilience focuses on the recovery, while tenacity focuses on never loosening the grip in the first place.

Tenacity is about the quality of the effort, not always the final result. A person can ultimately fail and still be described as having shown great tenacity — because what is being praised is the refusal to quit, the strength of character, not the outcome. That said, tenacity is most commonly mentioned in the context of success, precisely because it is often what causes people to succeed when others do not.
How it is used in sentences

Here are natural, common examples:

"She failed the bar exam three times but passed on the fourth attempt — a true display of tenacity."
"The team's tenacity in the final minutes of the game turned the match around."
"He pursued the investigation with tenacity, refusing to be dismissed or discouraged."
"Building a business from nothing requires enormous tenacity."

Common phrases you will encounter: show tenacity, demonstrate tenacity, with tenacity, remarkable tenacity, extraordinary tenacity, and tenacity of purpose (which means a sustained, focused drive toward one specific goal).

In older writing and some technical fields, tenacity can also describe the physical property of a material — its ability to resist breaking or tearing under pressure (for example, the tenacity of a steel wire). This usage is uncommon in everyday modern language, but it actually helps you feel the full weight of the word: just as a strong material holds together under force, a tenacious person holds together under the force of hardship.
The whole word in one sentence
Tenacity is the quality that makes a person keep going — firmly, persistently, and with deep inner strength — even when everything around them seems to say "stop."
